lessons.t: Tracing LLM and agent calls end to end
lessons.html:
A conventional service fails loudly. An AI feature usually fails with a 200 status, a well-formed response and a wrong answer. Often nothing in your code changed at all. Logs that record “request in, response out, 2.3 seconds” can’t tell you why. You need a trace: the full tree of steps one user request triggered, with enough detail on each step to replay and judge it.

For a retrieval-backed assistant the tree is short: guardrail check, retrieval, one model call, output validation. For an agent it can be fifty spans deep: a planning call, a dozen tool calls, results flowing back into context, a subagent with its own loop, a final answer. Each span is a place where quality, cost or latency went wrong.

What to capture per span

SpanRecordQuestion it answers
Model callModel ID the provider returned, prompt version, input, cached and output tokens, thinking tokens, time to first token, finish reasonWhich model and prompt produced this? Was the answer truncated? What did it cost?
RetrievalQuery, documents returned with scores, index versionWas the right answer ever in front of the model?
Tool callTool name, arguments, result size, error, durationDid the agent call the right tool with sane arguments?
GuardrailCheck name, verdict, scoreDid a filter block a good answer or pass a bad one?
Session rootUser or tenant ID, conversation ID, feature flag state, later feedback and eval scoresWhich users hit this, and was it good?

Record the model the provider returned as well as the one you requested. If you call an alias, the two can differ, and that difference is the first thing you’ll want during an incident.

The OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions

OpenTelemetry publishes semantic conventions for generative AI: standard span and attribute names so traces from different SDKs, frameworks and vendors line up. They define operations such as chat, embeddings, retrieval, execute_tool and invoke_agent, and attributes such as gen_ai.provider.name, gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.response.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and gen_ai.conversation.id. There are also conventions for MCP, metrics and events, plus provider-specific pages.

Two facts matter for planning. First, as of October 2026 the conventions are still marked Development status, and they now live in their own repository. Attribute names can still change, so pin your instrumentation version and keep the mapping to your dashboards in one place. Second, prompt and response content (gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages, gen_ai.system_instructions) is opt-in and flagged as likely to contain sensitive data. Whether you capture it, for whom, and for how long is a data-handling decision you make with security (Chapter 12), and it decides whether anyone can debug quality at all.

The trace is the bug report

A quality complaint without a trace ID is an anecdote. Build a way for support and users to attach the trace to every thumbs-down, and make “link the trace” the first line of every AI bug template.

Tracing also feeds everything else in this chapter. Upgrades are judged by replaying traces (lesson 3). Drift is spotted by comparing trace distributions over time (lesson 4). Cost per task in Chapter 11 is a sum over spans. If your traces are thin, every later step is guesswork.

What changes for you

  • Put a tracing requirement in every AI spec: the spans above, the returned model ID, prompt version, token counts and a trace ID visible to support.
  • Decide content capture explicitly: which surfaces log full prompts and outputs, the retention period and who can read them.
  • Start a weekly trace review: read 20 traces, including the five most expensive and the five slowest, alongside the Chapter 5 error analysis.

Every production AI feature needs three kinds of protection around the model: checks that stop bad inputs and outputs, a plan for when the model or provider is unavailable, and a way to spend less on easy requests. These are guardrails, fallbacks and cascades. They’re architecture decisions with direct product consequences, so the PM should be in the room.

Guardrails

A guardrail is a check that runs before, after or alongside the model and can block, rewrite or escalate.

  • Input: prompt-injection classifiers, PII detection, topic and abuse filters.
  • Output: schema validation, citation and grounding checks, policy classifiers, and deterministic business rules (“any price quoted must match the catalogue”).
  • Action: tool permissions, spend and step caps, human approval before irreversible actions (Chapter 6).

Prefer deterministic checks wherever the rule can be written as code. They’re cheap, fast and explainable. Use model-based classifiers for fuzzy policy. Every guardrail has a false-positive rate, and blocking a good answer is a product failure users feel. Measure each guardrail against your eval set for both misses and false blocks, and watch the added latency. Checks that run in parallel with generation, or on a streamed answer before it’s shown, cost less time than sequential ones.

Fallbacks

Providers have outages, rate limits (HTTP 429), slow periods and capacity errors. Plan the ladder in advance:

StepTriggerRisk to manage
1. Bounded retry with backoffTransient error or timeoutRetry storms multiply load and cost during an outage
2. Same model, other region or cloudRegional or provider-side failureDifferent data-residency terms and prices
3. Alternate modelSustained outage or rate limitDifferent behaviour; must pass the eval to qualify
4. Degraded modeAll models unavailableCached answers, search results or a non-AI path, clearly labelled
5. Honest failureNothing safe is availableA clear message and a way to retry later

An untested fallback is a second outage waiting. A fallback model is a model change, so it goes through the same eval gate as an upgrade, with its own prompt if needed. Rehearse switching to it.

Model cascades

A cascade sends each request to a cheap model first and escalates to a stronger one when a check fails or confidence is low. The arithmetic, with illustrative numbers: if a small model costs a tenth of the large one and handles 70% of traffic, the blended cost is 0.7 × 0.1 + 0.3 × (0.1 + 1.0) = 0.40 of sending everything to the large model. Escalated requests pay for both calls and take longer, so the saving depends on the escalation rate.

The escalation signal is the whole design

A cascade is only as good as its decision to escalate. A model’s self-reported confidence is often poorly calibrated. Prefer verifiable signals: the output parses, tests pass, retrieval scores clear a threshold, a calibrated judge approves. Measure how often the cheap model is wrong and doesn’t escalate, because those errors reach users.

A router is the cousin of a cascade: it classifies the request up front and sends it to one model. It saves the double call but needs a classifier you trust. Chapter 11 covers the economics.

What changes for you

  • For every guardrail in a spec, state what it blocks, its measured false-block rate on the eval set and its latency cost.
  • Require a written fallback ladder per feature, with each fallback model passing the eval before launch.
  • When a cascade is proposed, ask for the escalation signal and the rate of silent misses alongside the cost saving.

lessons.t: Model upgrades: pinning, shadow runs and rollout
lessons.html:
Model upgrades are the change you control least and that changes the most. A new model can be better on average and worse on your hardest 5%, more verbose, slower to first token, or refuse things the old one handled. Treat every model change as a release with its own pipeline.

Pin, then plan

Providers expose aliases (a name that points at the latest version) and pinned versions (an identifier that always means the same model). Use aliases in prototypes and pinned identifiers in production, so a change happens when you choose. Pinning doesn’t stop the clock. Providers retire models: Anthropic, for example, commits to at least 60 days’ notice before retiring a publicly released model and publishes tentative retirement dates on its deprecations page (as of October 2026). Keep a calendar of retirement dates for every model you depend on, including fallbacks.

What breaks beyond quality

  • API surface. Parameters get removed or change meaning. As of October 2026, Anthropic’s newer models reject non-default sampling parameters such as temperature, which breaks code that set them.
  • Tokens and cost. A new tokenizer or a chattier model changes token counts, cost and latency even at the same list price.
  • Format and tools. Different JSON habits, tool-calling patterns or stopping behaviour can break parsers and agent loops.
  • Refusals and tone. Safety tuning shifts, so some requests are newly refused or newly allowed.
  • Caches. Prompt caches don’t carry across models, so the first days after a switch cost more.

The rollout pipeline

StageTrafficWhat you measureExit criterion (illustrative)
Offline gateGolden set and regression suitePass rate, pass^k on critical cases, cost and latency per taskNo critical-case regressions; overall within 1 point
ShadowCopy of live traffic, output never shownPairwise judge preference, diff rates, format errors, token useJudge prefers new or ties on ≥ 90% of 500 samples
Canary1–5% of usersOnline metrics: acceptance, edits, retries, escalations, complaintsNo metric worse beyond its noise band after a week
Ramp25%, 50%, 100%The same, per segmentSegments hold; rollback still available
HoldOld model pinned as rollbackRetirement dateRemove only after the new model has run clean for a cycle

The Chapter 5 regression gate is the offline stage. Shadow runs catch what the golden set misses, because live traffic has a long tail no curated set covers. If you can’t shadow live traffic, replay a few hundred recent traces through the candidate.

Shadowing agents

A shadow agent must never act. Stub or sandbox every tool that writes, sends, pays or deletes, and point read tools at replicas where possible. Shadowing an agent with live write access is how teams send the same email twice.

Prompt changes, retrieval changes and tool-description changes go through the same pipeline. To users, they’re all model changes.

What changes for you

  • Name the pinned model identifier, its retirement date and the rollback model in every AI spec.
  • Make “offline gate, shadow, canary, ramp” the required release path for model and prompt changes, with exit criteria written before the run starts.
  • Put retirement dates on the roadmap a quarter ahead, so upgrades are scheduled work and never fire drills.

Drift is quality changing over time while your code and model stay the same. It’s the default state of an AI feature. Something always moves: what users ask, the world the answers describe, the data you retrieve, or the systems behind the API.

SourceExampleHow you detect it
Input driftA new product launch brings questions the prompt never anticipatedTopic and intent mix over time; rising fallback or refusal rates
World driftPrices, policies or regulations change; the index is staleFreshness checks on sources; spikes in “that’s out of date” feedback
Your own changesA prompt edit, a reindex, a changed tool API, a new guardrailChange log joined to trace metrics; regression gate on every change
Provider changesAn alias moves; serving or safety layers change behind a pinned nameA daily canary eval on a fixed set, compared with its own history

A canary eval is a small, fixed slice of your golden set (50 to 100 cases is typical) run on a schedule against production configuration. Because inputs never change, a move in its score points at the system. Pair it with sampled online evaluation of real traffic, which catches input drift the fixed set can’t.

The monitoring stack

  • System: error rate, 429s, timeouts, TTFT and end-to-end latency, cost per request and per task.
  • Behavioural proxies: acceptance, edits, retries, copy and regenerate rates, escalations to humans, refusal rate, and truncation (finish reason of max tokens).
  • Retrieval health: share of requests with empty or low-score retrieval.
  • Sampled quality: a calibrated judge scoring a fixed daily sample of traces against the rubric (Chapter 5).

Alert on rates and distributions, and leave individual outputs to the weekly review. Segment everything: an aggregate that holds steady can hide a collapse in one language, tenant or document type.

Incident response

AI incidents come in more shapes than outages, and severity should follow user harm.

IncidentTypical first signalFirst move
Hard outageError and timeout alertsFallback ladder; status message
Silent quality regressionCanary eval drop, rising edits or complaintsDiff recent changes; roll back the last model or prompt change
Cost spikeSpend per hour alert, token use per task jumpsCheck loops, retries, cache hit rate; cap spend
Harmful or embarrassing outputUser report, social media, judge flagKill switch or tighter guardrail; preserve traces
Data exposure or injectionSecurity alert, odd tool callsDisable the affected tool or surface; security lead takes over (Chapter 12)

Two capabilities decide how fast you recover. A kill switch per feature, and per tool for agents, that product can flip without a deploy. And replay: the ability to rerun an incident’s traces against a candidate fix before shipping it. Every postmortem ends with the failing cases added to the golden set, so the same failure can’t ship twice.

What changes for you

  • Ask for a daily canary eval and a segmented quality dashboard as a launch requirement.
  • Write AI incident severities in terms of user harm, and name who can flip each kill switch.
  • Close every AI postmortem by adding its cases to the golden set and the regression gate.

Service level objectives work for AI features if you extend them. The SRE vocabulary still applies: a service level indicator (SLI) is a measured quantity, a service level objective (SLO) is the target for it, and the error budget is how much you may miss before changes stop. What’s new is that quality becomes an SLI, and quality can only be measured on samples.

A worked set of SLOs

For an in-product assistant, with illustrative targets you would replace with your own baseline:

SLIMeasured onSLO (illustrative)
AvailabilityAll requests, excluding user errors99.5% of requests return a usable response, including fallbacks
Time to first tokenAll streamed requestsp95 under 2 seconds
End-to-end latencyAll requestsp95 under 12 seconds
Answer quality500 sampled traces per week, calibrated judge≥ 90% pass the rubric
GroundingSame sample≥ 97% of factual claims supported by a cited source
SafetyAll outputs via classifier, flags reviewed by humansFewer than 1 confirmed policy violation per 10,000 responses
CostAll tasksp95 cost per task under the budget set in Chapter 11

Sampling makes quality SLOs statistical

A quality SLO measured on a sample has error bars. With 500 samples and a true pass rate of 92%, the 95% confidence interval is about ±2.4 points (1.96 × √(0.92 × 0.08 ÷ 500)). A week at 90.5% is therefore not clear evidence of a breach. Set the sample size so the interval is narrower than the change you care about, and alert on sustained breaches or trends rather than one noisy reading. Rare events need different treatment: you can’t estimate a 1-in-10,000 safety rate from 500 samples, so safety SLIs run a classifier over all traffic and use humans to confirm the flags.

Also check the judge. If the calibrated judge drifts, or someone updates its prompt, your quality SLI moves with no change in the product. Version the judge like any other model and recalibrate it against human grades on a schedule.

Start from the baseline

Measure two to four weeks of real traffic first. An SLO set at demo quality is breached on day one and then ignored. An SLO set slightly above today’s baseline gives the team a target it can move.

Spending the error budget

The error budget is where SLOs earn their keep. Agree in advance what happens when the quality budget is spent: model, prompt and retrieval changes pause except fixes, and the next sprint goes to error analysis and the failing cases. When the budget is healthy, the team can take more risk, such as trying a cheaper model or a new capability. That turns arguments about whether quality is “good enough” into a rule everyone signed up to.

Segment the SLOs that matter most. A 92% pass rate overall can be 70% for one language or one enterprise tenant, and the aggregate SLO will never show it. Contractual commitments to customers belong on the segments they buy, which is one reason to keep external SLAs looser than internal SLOs.

What changes for you

  • Add quality, grounding and safety SLIs, with sample sizes and measurement method, to the non-functional section of every AI spec.
  • Get the error-budget policy agreed by product and engineering leads before launch.
  • Review SLO attainment per segment in the monthly business review, alongside cost per task.

lab.title: Write and rehearse a model upgrade playbook
lab.time: about 3 hours, plus a week of canary if you take it live
lab.intro: You’ll take one live feature through a real or simulated model change, using your Chapter 5 eval and shadow or replayed traffic. The lab proves you can change a model on purpose, measure the result, and roll back in minutes.
steps: Inventory. For one live feature, list every model it calls (including fallbacks and judges), the pinned identifier, the prompt version, the parameters set, and each model’s published retirement date. Note any model called by alias.

Pick a candidate. Choose the model you would move to next: a newer version, a cheaper tier or another provider. Read its migration notes and list any parameter, format or tool-calling changes your code depends on.

Run the offline gate. Run your Chapter 5 eval on current and candidate, three runs each. Record pass rate, pass^3 on critical cases, cost per task and p95 latency. Write the exit criteria before you look at results.

Shadow or replay. Send 500 live requests to the candidate in shadow, or replay 500 recent traces if you can’t shadow. Stub every tool that writes. Compare outputs with a calibrated pairwise judge and record format errors and token use.
Read 30 disagreements. Read the 30 cases where the judge preferred the current model most strongly. Classify each by cause and decide whether any is a blocker.
Plan the canary. Write the canary size (1–5%), duration, online metrics with their normal noise bands, and the rollback triggers. Name who decides at each ramp step.
Rehearse rollback. In staging, switch to the candidate and back using the same flag production would use. Time it. If it takes a deploy, fix that first.
Write the playbook. Fill in the template below and file it where on-call can find it.
lab.template:
FieldYour entry
Feature and owner
Current model (pinned ID) and retirement date
Candidate model and known API differences
Offline gate result: pass rate, pass^3 critical, cost per task, p95 latency (current → candidate)
Shadow result: judge preference, format errors, token change
Top three regressions from reading disagreements
Canary size, duration and online metrics watched
Rollback triggers (metric, threshold, window)
Rollback mechanism and measured time to roll back
Decision owner at each ramp step
lab.done: You have a filled-in playbook backed by real numbers, a rollback you’ve timed, and a go or no-go decision you could defend to engineering leadership. The next model change for this feature becomes a scheduled task.

quiz.q: Users report worse answers this week. No code, prompt or model identifier changed. Your daily canary eval on a fixed set is flat, but sampled judge scores on live traffic dropped. What’s the most likely explanation?
o: The provider silently changed the model
The judge model is broken
A cache outage
Input drift: users are asking different things than before
quiz.w: A flat canary on fixed inputs suggests the system itself is unchanged. A drop only on live traffic points at what users are sending, so look at the intent mix and recent product launches.

quiz.q: A team proposes a cascade: a small model answers first and escalates when it reports low confidence. What should you ask for before approving?
o: The share of requests where the small model is wrong and doesn’t escalate
The small model’s benchmark scores
The large model’s price per token
Whether the small model supports streaming
quiz.w: Self-reported confidence is often poorly calibrated. Silent misses reach users, so the escalation signal and its miss rate decide whether the cascade is safe.

quiz.q: You plan to shadow a new model on your support agent, which can issue refunds. What must be true before shadow traffic starts?
o: The new model is cheaper
The shadow agent’s write tools are stubbed or sandboxed so it can’t act
Users have consented to the new model
The shadow run uses temperature 0
quiz.w: A shadow agent must never take real actions. Stub refund and other write tools, or customers get double refunds.

quiz.q: Your weekly quality SLO is ≥ 90% pass on 500 sampled traces. This week shows 89.2%; the previous six weeks were 91–92%. What’s the right response?
o: Declare an incident and roll back the last change
Ignore it permanently
Treat it as within sampling noise, check for a trend or a segment collapse, and act if it persists
Raise the sample to 5,000 this week only
quiz.w: At n = 500 and a 90% rate the interval is about ±2.6 points, so one reading at 89.2% isn’t clear evidence of a breach. Look for trends and segment failures before acting.

quiz.q: Which statement about the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions was accurate as of October 2026?
o: They’re Stable, and full prompt content is captured by default
They only cover OpenAI models
They were replaced by MCP
They’re in Development status, and prompt and response content is opt-in
quiz.w: The conventions are marked Development and live in their own repository. Content attributes such as input and output messages are opt-in and flagged as sensitive.

quiz.q: Your provider announces your pinned model retires in 60 days. Your fallback model is the same family. What’s the most important first step?
o: Switch the alias to the latest model immediately
Check the fallback’s retirement date and schedule both upgrades through the offline gate, shadow and canary pipeline
Ask the provider for an extension
Fine-tune the old model
quiz.w: Retirements often hit a model family together. Treat both as scheduled releases through the full pipeline rather than switching blind.

deliverable.title: Runbook for model changes and AI incidents
deliverable.html:
A one-page runbook your on-call and product leads can use without you in the room. Keep it with the feature’s spec.

  1. Dependencies. Every model the feature calls (primary, fallbacks, guardrail classifiers, judges), with pinned identifier, owner and retirement date.
  2. Change pipeline. The stages a model, prompt or retrieval change must pass (offline gate, shadow, canary, ramp), with the exit criteria for each.
  3. SLOs and error budget. The SLIs, targets, sample sizes and the agreed policy when the budget is spent.
  4. Fallback ladder. Each step, its trigger and whether it has been rehearsed.
  5. Incident table. Incident types with severity defined by user harm, first signal, first move and the person who can flip each kill switch.
  6. Tracing and data. What is captured per span, whether content is logged, retention, and how support attaches a trace ID to a complaint.
  7. After an incident. Postmortem owner, and the rule that failing cases join the golden set before the incident closes.

Review it at every model upgrade and after every incident. If a step hasn’t been rehearsed in a quarter, mark it untested.
